Charles Colcock Jones
chärlz kol'kok jōnz
n. (Charles Colcock Jones, 1804–1863, Georgia Presbyterian minister and plantation catechist)
English patronymic Jones, son of John; Colcock a Carolina family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Charles Colcock Jones was a Liberty County, Georgia, planter who trained at Andover and Princeton and returned to spend his life catechizing the slaves of the Georgia low country. He preached to them on three plantations in rotation, wrote A Catechism of Scripture Doctrine and Practice for oral use with people forbidden to read, organised watchmen and classes drawn from among them, and published The Religious Instruction of the Negroes in the United States to press other owners to the same work. He taught at Columbia Seminary and served as secretary of the Presbyterian board of domestic missions. He was called in his own circles the apostle to the slaves, and the catechism he wrote was used for decades. He also owned the people he catechized, and freed none of them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, and to catechize as to instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers.

expand to see more

CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

CATECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.

MEN'STEALER, n. One who steals men; one who kidnaps.

Key Scripture

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

1Ti 1:10 — "For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;"

Deu 24:7 — "If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you."

Jer 22:13 — "Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;"

Modern Corruption

He taught the catechism to people he refused to free, and the catechism he taught condemned him.

expand to see more

Jones is the clearest case in American church history of a genuine religious labour built on an institution Scripture condemns outright. The instruction was real; so were the watchmen, the classes, and the forty years of riding between plantations. But Exo 21:16 fixes a capital penalty on the man who steals and sells a man, Deu 24:7 repeats it for Israel, and 1Ti 1:10 lists menstealers in the same breath as the lawless and the perjured. Jer 22:13 pronounces woe on him who “useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13), which is the plantation arrangement in six words.

The dictionary refuses both of the usual evasions. The first calls Jones a man of his time, as though the texts were unavailable to his time; he had Hebrew and Greek and read both. The second treats his catechetical work as cancelling the wrong, when in fact it aggravates it: he taught these people that God requires justice and withheld it from them himself. The lesson for the reader is that sincerity, industry, and sound doctrine on paper can coexist with a settled, defended, lifelong sin, and that the church which honoured him failed to put Exo 21:16 to him plainly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal; Greek andrapodistes (G405), a slave-dealer, menstealer; Hebrew sakar (H7939), wages.

Usage

"“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — the law he never applied to himself."

"“for menstealers, for liars” (1Ti 1:10) — the company Paul assigns."

"“useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13) — the woe pronounced."
